title: Where the seams go, and what each hop costs
description: Splitting the web tier from the application tier lets each scale on its own axis. Splitting further into services buys independence — and charges you latency and availability for every synchronous hop.

steps.text: The web tier terminates HTTP and holds no session state, so any instance can serve any request and the tier scales by changing a number.

It resolves a service name to a healthy instance. In practice the platform provides this — a Kubernetes service name resolving to healthy pods is server-side discovery with nothing to build. Knowing when the platform already solved it is part of the answer.
The call goes to a live instance. Orders is I/O-bound and Search is CPU-bound, so they scale on different axes — which is exactly the pressure that justified separating them.
Each service has exclusive access to its own store, and a different store where that fits — relational for orders, an index for search.

If two services read and write the same tables, they are not separate services. They are one service with a network hop in the middle, and they get the distributed failure modes with none of the independence.

Follow the data when choosing seams, then the team, then the change rate, then the scale profile. Splitting by technical layer — a 'database service', a 'validation service' — produces services that can never change independently, because every feature touches all of them.
Availability multiplies downward: six services at 99.9% in a synchronous chain ceiling at 99.4%, roughly two days a year lost to composition alone.
Latency accumulates per hop, and fan-out turns a rare slow response into a common slow page — a 1% p99 across 20 calls affects nearly one page in five.

And a transaction spanning two services stops being BEGIN/COMMIT and becomes a saga with compensating actions. That is usually the largest hidden cost. Start with a modular monolith and extract when a specific pressure justifies it — "we would split this out when X becomes true" is a stronger answer than a diagram with twelve services.
